candidate_findings.title: Focused-run state is not closed over zero, multiple, or changing active runs
candidate_findings.claim: The model defines one active_run_id and derives focus_mode by equality, while also acknowledging active background runs without defining their interaction with historical focus. It does not specify no-active-run behavior, multiple active/background-run cardinality, active-run rollover, race ordering, or which run live CTAs target during concurrent updates.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A run finishing, pausing, or being replaced while the user inspects history can silently change mode or send an action to the wrong run, producing misleading GUI truth or unintended runtime effects.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define the authoritative state owner; active-run cardinality; null and multiple-run states; transition events and ordering; persisted versus preview focus; atomic cross-tab propagation; active-run rollover; background-run selection; and stale-command rejection against an expected run/version.

evidence_refs.excerpt: `active_run_id` is the currently running, `/paused/interrupted`, or otherwise active run for the project; `focused_run_id` is the run shown by Orchestrator tabs

candidate_findings.title: Historical-mode status and tab propagation are internally inconsistent
candidate_findings.claim: The canonical section simultaneously presents Historical Run Mode as recommended or absent, later marks it accepted, requires all tabs to show the historical run, and then names only five of the seven active tabs as coherent consumers.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Plan Compile or Seams can display live/project state beside historical state without a deterministic disclosure rule, and implementers cannot tell whether the mode contract is settled or advisory.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Separate stale/advisory lineage from normative text and provide a per-tab historical-mode matrix for all seven tabs covering displayed run identity, available actions, disabled reasons, persistence, fallback, and switch-back-to-live behavior.

candidate_findings.title: The shared destination payload has no bounded schema or resolver failure contract
candidate_findings.claim: RGV-003 mandates one payload across many callers but does not define required discriminators, project/run binding, payload version, authorization checks, canonical resolver owner, or outcomes for malformed, stale, deleted, superseded, cross-project, or unauthorized targets.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Independent callers can encode the same destination differently, restore an approximate or wrong object, leak cross-project context, or execute a stale action after restart.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Specify a versioned discriminated payload schema; required project/run/generation/object identities; optional inspector/filter state; caller and resolver ownership; permission checks; canonicalization; expiry; invalid-target UX; stale-generation handling; backward compatibility; and deterministic route fixtures.

evidence_refs.excerpt: Run Graph uses one shared destination payload for search results, command-palette results, widget drill-downs, recovery links, resume URLs, artifact opens, subject-open semantics, and cross-surface pivots.

candidate_findings.title: Projection trust has disclosure language but no authoritative gating state machine
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt alternates among disclose, flag, may gate, and should disclose, without defining trust-state sources, thresholds, precedence, transitions, or an exact action matrix for stale and degraded data.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Two surfaces can show different trust claims or leave blocked/runtime actions enabled against stale truth, while a banner creates false assurance without enforced command behavior.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define trust-state enumeration and authority, freshness and degradation thresholds, source precedence, propagation latency, per-action allow/disable/reroute rules, stale-version preconditions, refresh and recovery transitions, fallback data provenance, and audit events.

evidence_refs.excerpt: disclose stale/degraded projection trust before showing live claims
`Seams`: allow browsing, but gate actions ... `Evidence`: artifact browsing can remain available; live verdict/action affordances may gate
live status claims, blocked action buttons, and generation overlays should disclose trust state explicitly

candidate_findings.title: Graph patch and safe-point retry actions lack concurrency, idempotency, and partial-failure semantics
candidate_findings.claim: Exact targeting and hard-gate labels are required, but the excerpt does not define who may invoke or approve these mutations, expected-generation/worktree preconditions, locking, idempotency, timeout, cancellation, retry deduplication, compensation, or recovery after only part of an operation succeeds.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A double-submit or stale inspector can apply a patch twice, race another generation, restore the wrong worktree state, or launch duplicate retries after an ambiguous timeout.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define command authority; confirmation and policy gates; expected generation, baseline, head and safe-point hashes; lock scope; idempotency keys; operation states; timeout/cancellation semantics; conflict and partial-success results; compensation; durable receipts; and post-command projection reconciliation.

evidence_refs.excerpt: `hard_gate` - approve/reject HITL boundaries - graph patch application when it changes canonical graph generation - remote-side-effect actions with explicit non-bypassable policy
apply accepted patch should likely be `hard_gate` or runtime-controlled strong action because it changes canonical graph generation
`restore_safe_point_then_retry` must carry exact worktree/baseline targeting rather than implied reuse

candidate_findings.title: Host access pivots omit URL threat controls and secret-handling rules
candidate_findings.claim: RGV-015 requires confidence, health, staleness, source, and authority disclosure, but gives no allowed schemes or hosts, redirect policy, credential stripping, private-network boundary, user-confirmation rule, provenance signature, or audit behavior. The prohibition applies only to silently auto-opening low-confidence URLs.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: A compromised or stale port_access_record could expose credentials, open an attacker-controlled destination, pivot into localhost or a private network, or bind an action to the wrong container.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define URL canonicalization and allowlists; redirect validation; credential/query-fragment redaction; private-address policy; instance and project binding; confidence-independent confirmation for external effects; permission checks; stale revocation; provenance verification; safe rendering/copy behavior; and audited denial reasons.

candidate_findings.title: Inspector disclosure fields have no field-level access or redaction policy
candidate_findings.claim: The inspector exposes account, persona, usage/cost, worktree/snapshot, SCM identity, evidence and artifact data, yet the excerpt provides no viewer-role matrix, artifact ACL inheritance, path masking, secret scrubbing, copy/export rule, or privacy-safe fallback.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Shared screens, logs, screenshots, deep links, or lower-privilege viewers can reveal account identity, costs, local paths, repository topology, artifact contents, or embedded credentials.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Specify field classification, viewer permissions, account pseudonymization, path and URL redaction, evidence/artifact authorization inheritance, secret scanning, copy/export and telemetry rules, denied-field placeholders, and audit logging.

candidate_findings.title: Provider-family identity uses two incompatible field names and omits unresolved-attempt states
candidate_findings.claim: The data-model sentence says it records provider_family but then constrains provider_family_id, leaving the canonical key ambiguous. It also covers only attempts that resolved through provider routing without specifying the inspector state for unresolved, failed, cancelled, legacy, or partially migrated attempts.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Producers and consumers can serialize different keys, lose grouping identity, or falsely omit failed routing attempts from the graph and cost/account audit trail.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Choose one canonical field and type; define aliases and migration precedence; specify nullability and invariants; model requested, resolving, resolved, failed, cancelled and legacy states; and provide round-trip fixtures rejecting conflicting values.

candidate_findings.title: Concern creation and lifecycle remain proposed while the graph consumes concern references
candidate_findings.claim: The excerpt permits real concerns to be minted and requires concern references in graph detail, but concern canonicalization, owner authority, status transitions, resolution/dismissal permissions, merge/split behavior, and idempotent nomination are still discussion items or directives to define later.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: The graph can display duplicate, orphaned, prematurely resolved, or noncanonical concerns and cannot deterministically distinguish acknowledgement from semantic closure.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define the concern owner and canonical store; nomination-to-canonical transition; stable identity and deduplication; allowed status transitions and actors; resolution and dismissal evidence; merge/split/supersession lineage; optimistic concurrency; retention; and read-only behavior until authority exists.

candidate_findings.title: Large-graph mechanisms lack quantitative limits and truth-preserving invariants
candidate_findings.claim: The graph is expected to handle thousands of nodes using culling, caching, throttling, virtualization and level-of-detail reduction, but there are no node/edge limits, frame or interaction budgets, update rates, backpressure policy, cache invalidation rules, deterministic layout requirement, or invariant that selected, blocked, failed and newly changed objects remain discoverable.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: At scale the UI can silently omit critical blockers, present stale overlays, thrash memory, or produce nondeterministic screenshots and navigation, while still claiming full lineage is available.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Set supported node/edge and generation bounds; latency, frame-time and memory budgets; event-rate/backpressure behavior; cache keys and invalidation; LOD visibility priorities; search completeness; deterministic layout/selection rules; degraded-mode disclosure; and scale fixtures with measurable pass/fail thresholds.

the graph is expected to handle very large scale (thousands of nodes)

candidate_findings.title: Tier-era retirement has no deterministic compatibility translation
candidate_findings.claim: Tier tokens are declared compatibility aliases or source lineage only, but the excerpt does not define how old bookmarks, persisted page state, commands, telemetry, copied tier IDs, or tier-keyed records translate, fail, warn, or retire.
candidate_findings.why_it_matters: Legacy routes can silently open an approximate node or wrong attempt, historical records can become unreachable, and compatibility behavior can persist indefinitely without a measurable retirement gate.
candidate_findings.missing_contract: Define a versioned tier-to-node/attempt mapping; ambiguity and one-to-many handling; unsupported-route UX; no-silent-fallback rule; persisted-state migration; telemetry and deprecation phases; retention requirements; retirement criteria; and compatibility fixtures.
